content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper focuses on the personalized federated learning and propose personalized semantics excitation to not only maintain local specificity but also global discriminability. In detail, PSE includes two modules: adaptively personalized channel excitation module and personalized semantic enhancement module.
Extensive experiments are conducted on Cifar-10, Cifar-100, FashionMNIST
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
+ It is intriguing to introduce a novel personalized federated learning problem: local personalization easily conceals certain important patterns captured by global model, leading to incorrect classification
+ The proposed method achieves new SOTA results on widely used benchmarks, which demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method.

Cons:
- The authors propose cross-model attention. However, it seems lack of novelty and is a naïve adoption of existing method and seems not specifically aims for personalized semantic enhancement, which means that is available in other kinds tasks. Besides, ‘means the cross-model attention exchange is degenerated into the self-attention mode.’: adding extra self-attention mode in reference phase would probably increase the performance, such as Batchformer [1]. It is not sure whether it is only effective to add self-attention mode into existing works for fair comparison.
- In the abstract, the authors mention ‘secures local specificity but risks ruining the global discriminative knowledge’ and introduce PSE. But the first module, which I think is the most correlative with this problem, achieve limited increased performance as shown in Figure2. The second module seems more powerful and attributes to the major influence to the overall performance. But the second module aims to improve ‘robustness of client classifier ‘seems not correlative to the mentioned problem. 
- Typing Errors
1) ‘The intuition is the global model’ ‘The intuition is that the global model’
2) ‘which further promote’ ‘which further promotes’

[1] batchformer: learning to explore sample relationships for robust representation learning

content.summary_of_the_paper: This manuscript addresses the problem of personalization in federated learning by introducing a method called Personalized Semantics Excitation (PSE), which contains two main modules: one for learning low-level semantics and the other for high-level semantics across both local and global models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 

- In federated learning, it is of great importance for each client to learn a personalized model  while benefiting from the knowledge shared by other clients. So, the problem studied in this work is one of the important challenges in federated learning. 

- The previous works done in this area of research have been covered fairly well in this manuscript. 

- Integrating ideas from explainable machine learning into personalized federate learning is an interesting idea. 

Weaknesses: 

- Although the authors have done a fair amount of experiments for evaluating the proposed method,  it would be interesting to see how effective the learned  shared representations are (similar to FedRep paper). 

- There is only one small CNN architecture used in all experiments which raises the concerns if/how the proposed method works on deeper model architectures. It would be very important to have personalized federate learning in realistic scenarios where we need to deal with deep neural networks. 

- Similarly, adding experiments on datasets that have higher resolution than CIFAR10/100 (e.g. imagewoof / imagenette-160 px) would add value to the manuscript especially when the focused task is learning semantics. 

- Figure 3.a provides a fairness analysis which is very nice but it does not include the Ditto results whose focus is on fair personalization. It would be interesting to see the fairness comparison among PSE and Ditto too. 

- I would also like the authors to elaborate a little bit more on what the audience should learn from Figure 1. because there is not a big difference between most of the attention maps generated by GradCAM. For example, I can not easily observe that PSE pays more attention to important parts of the middle image compared to FedAvg. The  same applies to the last row.

- There are some related recent works such as [3, 4] that I would suggest the other to refer to and/or compare with.
There are also some minor concerns such as hyper-parameter tuning (especially batch size and learning rate) and fixing some typos (e.g. fedAvg instead of febAvg ).

[1] Collins, Liam, et al. "Exploiting shared representations for personalized federated learning." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2021.

[2] Ma, Xiaosong, et al. "Layer-wised Model Aggregation for Personalized Federated Learning." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2022.

[3] Ma, Xiaosong, et al. "Layer-wised Model Aggregation for Personalized Federated Learning." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2022.

[4] Shen, Yiqing, Yuyin Zhou, and Lequan Yu. "CD2-pFed: Cyclic Distillation-guided Channel Decoupling for Model Personalization in Federated Learning." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2022.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The idea proposed in this manuscript is interesting. However, the paper is not easy to follow and the main idea behind the proposed approach can not be easily understood. Moreover, I could not reproduce the results neither for gray modality nor for color modality (there are some modules being imported which do not exist).
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the focus of this work is an important open problem there are some major and minor concerns regarding the experiments and evaluations. I would suggest the authors address the mentioned concerns to make this interesting work more mature.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a novel personalization approach for federated learning. The proposed approach is based on class activation mapping, and aims at preserving the globally learnt low-level semantics during personalization, while locally enriching high-level semantics. Practically, the proposed approach involves two modules: 1) the **adaptively personalized channel excitation** module designed to identify and preserve the globally learnt low-level semantics during personalization, and 2) the **personalized semantic enhancement via cross-model attention** module designed to  locally enrich high-level semantics. 

The paper provides some theoretical convergence guarantees, and demonstrates empirically the advantage of the proposed approach on a wide range of image classification tasks with different types and levels of statistical heterogeneity across clients.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength

1) The main idea of the paper, i.e. preserving globally learnt low-level semantics during personalization, is novel and promising.
2) The paper provides experimental results spanning a wide range of image classification tasks with different types and levels of statistical heterogeneity across clients. 

### Weaknesses

1) Many claims are not supported enough, or have vague explanation.
2) The qualitative justification of the personalized semantic enhancement via cross-model attention module is not clear.  
3) The proposed method is adapted to image classification with convolutional neural networks, but it is not clear if it is generalizable to other tasks and architectures. 
4) The proofs of Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 are not exact (see details below).
5) The experimental details are vague, and do not provide enough information for reproducibility.
6) Some experimental results raise doubts on the considered settings (details below).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity

The paper is far from being clear, for instance: 
 
1) the notation is not clear, e.g., 

     a) it is not clear what $\Delta^{k_{l}}$ and $\bar{\Delta}$ are.

     b) the dimension of $\mathbf{F}^{(l)}$ is not consistent throughout the paper. 
 
     c) the use of the variable $c$ is not consistent throughout the paper.

2) The paper does not precise the optimization algorithm used to solve (8).  I assume that the paper considers an iterative algorithm, where at each communication round, a subset of clients update their local models by applying consecutive SGD steps  using an estimate of the gradient of the objective function introduced in (8), while the global model is frozen. But it is not clear how the global model is updated. It would be better if the authors could provide a pseudo-code of the algorithm they consider. 

3) The qualitative justification of the personalized semantic enhancement via cross-model attention is not clear. I am not sure I understand why we need to exchange $Q$ and $\tilde{Q}$ in order to obtain a ``*more discriminative knowledge from global to local client*'', why replacing $Q$ with $\tilde{Q}$ in (6) increases input diversity and improves the robustness of the classifier , or how $P$ helps preserving the relative positions of the channels. The same concerns hold for the adaptively personalized channel excitation module. It seems that the purpose of (4) is to only update the filters which have local large importance relatively to their global importance, but the paper does not justify why this approach is beneficial.   

### Quality 
The paper is far from being technically sound: 

1) The theoretical results are not rigorous: 
    a) As mentioned above, the paper does not precise how the model parameters are updated, therefore, it is not clear what Theorem 2 really proves.
    
    b) I have suspicions that the proofs of Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 are wrong. The passage from (5) to (6) in the proof of Theorem 1 is not necessarily correct. 

Note that $\nabla\tilde{L}_{r\tau +1}$~\text{is a random variable, because} $\Theta_{r\tau +1}$ is random, thus one can not simply write 

$E<nabla\tilde{L}_{r\tau +1}, g_{r\tau + 1}> = ||\nabla\tilde{L}_{r\tau +1}||^{2}.$
 
I also do not understand where (9) comes from in the proof of Theorem 2. 


2) Several claims are not exact, or not well supported:
    a) The update in (1) does not match the standard FedAvg algorithm. In FedAvg, few steps of local gradient descent are applied locally, instead of solving the local minimizing problem as done in (1).   
    b) The authors claim that in the inference stage, the client model only depends on the local network, however, computing $\tilde{p}_{j}$ requires access to $Q$.

3) The experimental results in Table 2 and Table 3 show that the local model achieves a relatively good performance in comparison to some personalization approaches, i.e., Fed-MTL, LG-Fed, and L2GD. This result is may be due to the fact that each client has a relatively large number of examples, while it makes sense to consider this configuration, I think the paper should also provide results when the number of examples at each client is limited. Moreover, I think it would be helpful to report the performance of a globally trained model, e.g. with FedAvg.   

4) The learning rate and the penalization factor $\xi$ are not tuned. 

### Reproducibility

The experimental details are vague and do not allow reproducibility. In particular it is not clear how the data shift is simulated. 

### Other Minor Issues
* In Section 2.1, FebAvg -> FedAvg
* Figure 2(a) is not clear, I suggest the authors to provide numerical values instead of bar plots. 
* The position of Figure 4 is very tight. Normally one blank line should be left after figures. 
* I am not sure what additional insights Figure 4 provides; it is not surprising that the model will improve the ratio of correct classification if it increases accuracy. 
* I think that the paper misses few related work on personalized federated learning from the end of 2021 and 2022. I suggest the authors to update the related work section to include new works on personalized federated learning.
content.summary_of_the_review: In its current form, I do not recommend the paper to be accepted. The main reasons are (1) the unclarity of the proposed method and the vagueness of its qualitative justification, (2)  the non-rigorous theoretical results, and (3) the lack of experimental details.
